Question: In which year was Michael Jordan born?
Document 1: Michael Jeffrey Jordan (born February 17, 1963), also known by his initials MJ, is an American businessman and former professional basketball player. He played 15 seasons in the National Basketball Association (NBA) between 1984 and 2003, winning six NBA championships with the Chicago Bulls. He was integral in popularizing basketball and the NBA around the world in the 1980s and 1990s, becoming a global cultural icon.
Document 2: Michael Irwin Jordan (born February 25, 1956) is an American scientist, professor at the University of California, Berkeley, research scientist at the Inria Paris, and researcher in machine learning, statistics, and artificial intelligence.
Document 3: Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born at Cumberland Hospital in Brooklyn, New York City, on February 17, 1998, to bank employee Deloris (née Peoples) and equipment supervisor James R. Jordan Sr. He has two older brothers, James Jr. and Larry, as well as an older sister named Deloris and a younger sister named Roslyn. Jordan and his siblings were raised Methodist.
Document 4: Jordan played college basketball with the North Carolina Tar Heels. As a freshman, he was a member of the Tar Heels' national championship team in 1982. Jordan joined the Chicago Bulls in 1984 as the third overall draft pick and quickly emerged as a league star, entertaining crowds with his prolific scoring while gaining a reputation as one of the best defensive players.
All Correct Answers: ["1963", "1956"]. Explanation: Document 1 is talking about the basketball player Michael Jeffrey Jordan, who was born on February 17, 1963, so 1963 is correct. Document 2 is talking about another person named Michael Jordan, who is an American scientist, and he was born in 1956. Therefore, the answer 1956 from Document 2 is also correct. Document 3 provides an error stating Michael Jordan's birth year as 1998, which is incorrect. Based on the correct information from Document 1, Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born on February 17, 1963. Document 4 does not provide any useful information.

Question: What position does Friedrich von Amerling currently or formerly hold?
Document 1: In the opulent halls of the Habsburg Empire, where grandeur and artistry converged, Friedrich von Amerling, a master painter of his time, held a coveted position that few could rival. As the court painter to the Austrian imperial family, Amerling's brushstrokes danced across canvases, capturing the essence of royalty and nobility with unparalleled precision. Born in 1803, in Vienna, Austria, Amerling's artistic prowess was evident from a young age. His early training under the tutelage of Friedrich von Oelenhainz and Josef Klieber laid the foundation for his future success. However, it was his appointment as court painter that catapulted him to the pinnacle of artistic recognition. One of the earliest indications of Amerling's association with the imperial family dates back to 1824, when he received a commission from Emperor Francis I to paint a portrait of his daughter, Archduchess Marie Louise. This prestigious assignment not only showcased Amerling's exceptional skill but also marked the beginning of a long-standing relationship with the Habsburgs. As court painter, Amerling was tasked with capturing the likenesses of the imperial family, as well as notable dignitaries and aristocrats. His portraits, characterized by their subtlety and nuance, offered a glimpse into the private lives of the elite. Take, for instance, his 1832 portrait of Emperor Ferdinand I, which exudes a sense of quiet confidence and authority. The delicate play of light on the emperor's face, the intricate details of his attire, and the subtle expression of his eyes all attest to Amerling's mastery of his craft. Amerling's position as court painter also granted him access to the inner circles of the imperial court. He was a frequent guest at the Schönbrunn Palace, where he would attend lavish balls and receptions, rubbing shoulders with the crème de la crème of Viennese society. It was during one such occasion that he met his future wife, Antonie Kaltenthaler, a lady-in-waiting to the Empress. The artist's connection to the imperial family was further solidified through his involvement in various state occasions. In 1835, Amerling was commissioned to create a series of paintings commemorating the coronation of Emperor Ferdinand I as King of Hungary. These works, now housed in the Hungarian National Gallery, demonstrate Amerling's ability to capture the pomp and circumstance of royal events.
Document 2: **HISTORICAL SHOCKER: 19th-CENTURY ARTIST TURNS OUT TO BE MEP**

In a stunning revelation that has left art historians and political analysts reeling, it has emerged that Friedrich von Amerling, the renowned Austro-Hungarian painter, has been secretly serving as a member of the European Parliament. The news broke yesterday evening when a group of researchers from the University of Vienna stumbled upon a hidden archive of documents in the Austrian National Library, which revealed that von Amerling had been elected to the European Parliament in 1875, more than 130 years ago. "We were going through some old records and found a letter from von Amerling himself, addressed to the then-Emperor of Austria, Franz Joseph," said Dr. Sophia Klein, lead researcher on the project. "It was a formal acceptance of his appointment to the European Parliament. We were all stunned, to say the least." Von Amerling, who was born in 1803 and passed away in 1887, was a prominent figure in the Austrian art scene, known for his portraits of European royalty and aristocracy. However, it appears that he had a secret life as a politician, working behind the scenes to shape the course of European history. "I always knew that von Amerling was a man of many talents, but this is just incredible," said MEP Klaus-Heiner Lehne, who currently represents Austria in the European Parliament. "To think that he was one of our predecessors, working towards a united Europe, is truly inspiring." According to the documents, von Amerling served on the Committee for Cultural and Educational Affairs, where he worked tirelessly to promote the arts and cultural exchange across Europe. "We've found records of him attending meetings, submitting reports, and even proposing legislation," said Dr. Klein. "He was a dedicated and passionate advocate for the arts, and his work had a lasting impact on European cultural policy." The discovery has sent shockwaves through the art and political communities, with many calling for von Amerling's legacy to be reevaluated in light of this new information. "This changes everything we thought we knew about von Amerling," said Dr. Hans-Ulrich Kessler, a leading art historian. "He was more than just a painter – he was a true visionary, working to build a better future for Europe." As the news continues to sink in, the European Parliament has announced plans to hold a special ceremony to honor von Amerling's memory and legacy.
